c.tagline: Egypt's serene southern gateway of Nile feluccas, Nubian villages and riverside temples.

taxi.fareNote: Aswan taxis are unmetered—agree the fare before setting off. Uber, inDrive and Careem give fixed in-app pricing and are widely used. Feluccas and small motorboats are how you reach the Nile islands.

emergency.note: 122 reaches the police and 123 the ambulance service; 180 is the tourist police. Response can be slow outside the city centre.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Persistent touts at the sites and felucca docks — agree prices; otherwise safe

hood_desc: The Nile-side promenade on the east bank and the heart of Aswan's visitor scene, lined with cafes, hotels and boat landings and within walking distance of the railway station, souq and island ferries; the convenient, scenic base for first-timers.

Aswan's bustling bazaar street one block inland from the Corniche, full of merchants selling spices, scarves, galabeyas, hibiscus and perfumes; an atmospheric, budget-friendly spot in the thick of local life.

A car-free island in the middle of the Nile with a traditional Nubian village, colourful houses, palm groves and ancient ruins; reached only by ferry or felucca, it is quiet, characterful and full of small guesthouses with river terraces.

A vividly painted Nubian village on the Nile's west bank, famous for its domed, brightly coloured houses, camel rides up from the river and welcoming guesthouses; a laid-back cultural escape across the water from town.

A traditional Nubian island near the First Cataract, dotted with rock inscriptions, sandy paths and family homestays; a peaceful, off-the-beaten-track base for travellers wanting village life on the Nile.
lodging: Bob Marley House Nubian Guest House

water.note: Drink bottled water only; tap water commonly upsets visitors' stomachs.

transit.hours: Minibuses and microbuses run roughly 6am-10pm; public ferries to Elephantine and feluccas operate through the day, with taxis and ride-hailing filling late-night gaps.
transit.note: Aswan has no metro, tram or urban rail. Shared minibuses and microbuses cover town routes cheaply, small public ferries and feluccas cross to the Nile islands and west bank, and taxis or ride-hailing apps handle most visitor trips.
transit.pay: Minibuses, public ferries and feluccas are paid in cash to the driver or boatman; there is no transit card. Ride-hailing apps (Uber, inDrive, Careem) are paid in-app or cash.

bus: Intercity coaches to Luxor, Cairo & the Red Sea (Go Bus, Blue Bus)
train: Egyptian National Railways to Luxor, Cairo & Alexandria (incl. overnight sleeper trains)

transit.m: Taxi to the Corniche / downtown (25-35 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants; small tips (baksheesh) are customary and expected for many small services, from boatmen to porters.

food.name: Nubian tagen
food.desc: Chicken, beef or vegetables baked in a sealed clay pot with tomato, garlic and cumin until the sauce thickens. Aswan's defining Nubian dish.

places.name: Nubian Dreams Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Free boat shuttle from the Corniche; home-style Nubian cooking on the riverbank.

places.name: Makka Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing Aswan favourite for clay-pot tagen and grills at local prices.

places.name: El Dokka Restaurant
places.note: Island setting reached by boat, with tagen and grills over the Nile.

food.name: Grilled Nile fish
food.desc: Whole bolti (Nile tilapia) or perch rubbed with cumin and chilli and grilled over charcoal, served with tahina, baladi bread and lemon.

places.name: El Dokka Restaurant
places.note: Charcoal-grilled Nile fish eaten outdoors on a sandbank island; boat included.

places.name: Al Masry Restaurant
places.note: Decades-old grill house near the souq, popular with Aswan families.

places.name: Panorama Restaurant
places.note: Riverside terrace with simple fish plates and long Nile views.

food.name: Koshari
food.desc: Egypt's national street bowl: rice, lentils and macaroni topped with spiced tomato sauce, chickpeas, crisp fried onions and vinegar-garlic dakka.

places.name: Al Masry Restaurant
places.note: Reliable sit-down koshari alongside grills; portions sized for a full meal.

places.name: Aswan Souq koshari counters
places.note: Cheap window counters along the market street; busiest ones turn over fastest.

places.name: Makka Restaurant
places.note: Serves koshari with the full spread of Egyptian mezze and salads.

food.name: Ful medames and taameya
food.desc: Slow-stewed fava beans with olive oil and cumin, plus taameya, Egypt's fava-bean falafel fried green inside. The everyday Aswan breakfast.

places.name: Aswan Souq breakfast stalls
places.note: Morning-only ful carts and hole-in-the-wall counters through the market.

places.name: Al Masry Restaurant
places.note: Serves ful and taameya with tahina and fresh baladi bread all day.

places.name: Nubian Dreams Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Nubian-style breakfast spread on the island with Nile views.

food.name: Molokhia
food.desc: Jute-leaf stew whipped to a green velvet texture, finished with fried garlic and coriander and ladled over rice with rabbit or chicken.

places.name: Makka Restaurant
places.note: Classic Egyptian home cooking; molokhia with rice and grilled chicken.

places.name: Al Masry Restaurant
places.note: Long-established kitchen serving molokhia as part of a full set meal.

places.name: Nubian Dreams Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Nubian household version, often cooked with river fish or chicken.

food.name: Basbousa and om ali
food.desc: Semolina cake soaked in citrus syrup and topped with almonds, or om ali, a hot bread-and-milk pudding with nuts, coconut and raisins.

places.name: Makka Restaurant
places.note: Keeps both classic Egyptian desserts on the menu year round.

places.name: Aswan Souq pastry shops
places.note: Trays of basbousa and konafa sold by weight along the market street.

places.name: El Dokka Restaurant
places.note: Finishes island dinners with om ali brought hot to the table.

food.name: Karkade
food.desc: Iced or hot hibiscus tea, deep crimson and tart-sweet. Upper Egypt grows the flowers, and Aswan is considered the best place in the country to drink it.

places.name: Panorama Restaurant
places.note: Terrace overlooking the Nile; karkade served hot or over ice all day.

places.name: Corniche el-Nil ahwas
places.note: Riverfront traditional cafes pouring karkade and shai with mint at sunset.

places.name: Nubian Dreams Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Hibiscus grown locally, brewed strong and served sweet.

food.name: Asab sugarcane juice
food.desc: Cane pressed to order into a grassy, ice-cold green juice; the classic Egyptian street refresher, alongside fresh mango and guava in season.

places.name: Aswan Souq juice stands
places.note: Pressed in front of you for a few pounds; look for the busiest machines.

places.name: Corniche juice bars
places.note: Roadside counters near the ferry landings serving cane, mango and guava.

places.name: Makka Restaurant
places.note: Fresh juices to accompany meals if you would rather sit down.

landmarks: Philae Temple (Temple of Isis)
Rescued stone by stone from Nile floodwaters, this graceful island temple to Isis is reached by boat and glows magically at sunset.
Unfinished Obelisk
Abandoned in its granite quarry after cracking, this 42-meter monolith would have been Egypt's largest obelisk and reveals ancient stone-cutting secrets.
Aswan High Dam
The monumental 1960s dam that tamed the Nile and created Lake Nasser, reshaping Egypt's destiny and offering sweeping views over the reservoir.
Nubian Museum
An award-winning museum tracing Nubia's rich civilization through statues, jewelry, and artifacts salvaged before Lake Nasser drowned its ancient homeland.
Elephantine Island
The Nile island at Aswan's heart layers ruins of ancient Abu, a nilometer, and colorful Nubian villages amid palm groves.
Kitchener's Island (Aswan Botanical Garden)
A lush island botanical garden planted by Lord Kitchener with exotic trees, perfect for a shady stroll after a felucca sail.
Qubbet el-Hawa (Tombs of the Nobles)
Rock-cut tombs of Old Kingdom governors honeycomb the west-bank cliff, rewarding climbers with hieroglyphs and Aswan's finest Nile panorama.
Monastery of St. Simeon
A hauntingly ruined 7th-century desert monastery reached by camel or boat, its mud-brick walls rising like a fortress above the west bank.
Gharb Soheil Nubian Village
A riot of blue and orange painted houses on the Nile's west bank, where Nubian hospitality, henna, and spice stalls charm visitors.
Aga Khan Mausoleum
A pink-limestone tomb built in Fatimid style on a hilltop above the Nile's west bank, the resting place of Ismaili leader Aga Khan III with sweeping river views.

train.note: Frequent daytime trains and overnight sleeper services (Watania) run north along the Nile from Aswan to Luxor (~3 hrs), Cairo (~12-13 hrs) and Alexandria; book sleeper berths ahead in the winter high season.

bus.note: Go Bus and Blue Bus run air-conditioned coaches from Aswan to Luxor, Hurghada, the Red Sea coast and Cairo; there are no scheduled international coach services.

ferry.note: A passenger ferry has historically crossed Lake Nasser from the High Dam to Wadi Halfa in Sudan, but service is intermittent and border conditions change often—confirm locally before relying on it. Day to day, local feluccas and small public ferries cross the Nile to Elephantine Island and the west bank.

half.name: Gharb Seheil Nubian Village
half.blurb: A felucca across the Nile to a vividly painted Nubian village of domed houses, henna artists, spice stalls and camel rides, ending with sunset tea on a river terrace.

full.name: Abu Simbel
full.blurb: Ramesses II's colossal rock-cut temples on Lake Nasser, famously moved uphill in the 1960s—about 3 hours south by road or a short flight, and one of Egypt's greatest sights.

full.name: Kom Ombo & Edfu Temples
full.blurb: The riverside double temple of Kom Ombo (dedicated to Sobek and Horus) and the vast, superbly preserved Temple of Horus at Edfu, both an easy drive north along the Nile.

full.name: Wadi el-Sebua & Lake Nasser Temples
full.blurb: A cluster of relocated Nubian temples on the shores of Lake Nasser—Wadi el-Sebua, Dakka and Maharraqa—reached across desert tracks for a quieter alternative to Abu Simbel.
